inspection_summary: The complete normalized article was inspected through its appended journal matter. Its reusable semantic chain is: state the elliptic-curve point-count bound; construct a pole-weighted function on the rational-point group over a self-composite function field; prove its quadraticity from local nonarchimedean valuation identities and the product formula; derive positive semidefiniteness from nonnegativity on an integer lattice; and evaluate the resulting discriminant on a point and its Frobenius image by classifying finite primes. Several displayed formulas are OCR-damaged, so units retain only relationships recoverable from checked prose and mark dependencies on the scan.

accepted_units.title: Elliptic point-count bound reduced to positivity of a quadratic form
accepted_units.why_material: The source states the analogue as |N-q| bounded by 2 square-root q, contrasts characteristic-restricted elementary proofs with a valuation-theoretic proof for all finite characteristics, and identifies positive semidefiniteness of a quadratic form as the stronger intermediate target.
accepted_units.context_note: The span includes the curve, finite field, point-count notation, historical comparison, and the announced proof architecture, so the strategic reduction is not detached from its hypotheses.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: Moderate: some equation glyphs are degraded, but the bound and positivity strategy are recoverable from the prose and displayed theorem.

accepted_units.title: Prime-divisor valuations and the additive product formula
accepted_units.why_material: The construction expands the prime divisors of k(x) to K, normalizes their discrete valuations, records the sharp ultrametric rule and finite support, and invokes the additive product formula with residue-degree multiplicities; these are the local-to-global ingredients later used to prove quadraticity.
accepted_units.context_note: This is setup for d and for the cancellation in lines 342-364, not an independent proof of the point-count theorem.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: High for exact transcription: displayed product formula (5) is absent from the text layer, although its role, additive form, and multiplicities are stated in prose; scan verification is needed before formula-level reuse.

accepted_units.title: Self-composite curve and its K-rational point group
accepted_units.why_material: The article passes from the original curve over k to the same elliptic equation over K as constant field, making its K-rational points into an abelian group whose coordinate addition formulas can be analyzed valuation by valuation.
accepted_units.context_note: This representation change supplies both the group on which d lives and the later distinguished point (x,y); the detailed addition laws are supporting machinery.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: High: the displayed addition and doubling formulas are substantially OCR-damaged, while the prose still clearly supplies the curve, rational-point group, and equality x_P=x_{-P}; exact formulas require scan verification.

accepted_units.title: Pole-weighted function and the parallelogram target
accepted_units.why_material: The source defines d(P) as a residue-degree-weighted sum over primes where x_P has a pole, uses finite support to make it well-defined, and identifies the parallelogram identity as the condition that makes d a quadratic form on the rational-point group.
accepted_units.context_note: The source notes that only two special points would suffice for the final bound, but proves the identity for arbitrary points, yielding a reusable global object.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: Moderate: definition (9) and identity (10) are recoverable; the expanded polarization formula (11) is OCR-damaged and should not be relied on verbatim.

accepted_units.title: Pole behavior under elliptic-curve addition
accepted_units.why_material: Lemma 1 shows that adding two points with negative x-valuations preserves a pole and controls its valuation, while adding a pole point to a non-pole point yields a non-pole; the proof uses the sharp ultrametric rule, the addition formula, and decompositions such as P=(P+Q)-Q.
accepted_units.context_note: The span includes the coefficient-valuation hypotheses and zero-point convention required for the lemma, as well as the equal-valuation argument rather than only its statement.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: Moderate: comparison symbols are imperfect in places, but the case structure and conclusions are stated in prose; exact displayed addition formula remains scan-dependent.

accepted_units.title: Valuations of P-Q and P+Q tied to coordinate separation
accepted_units.why_material: Lemma 2 separates the non-pole and pole cases for P and Q and relates the x-valuations of P-Q and P+Q to the valuation of x_P-x_Q, providing the local equality that later converts the sum defining d into a parallelogram identity.
accepted_units.context_note: The restriction P not equal to plus or minus Q and the specialization back to valuations of the original function field are included; exceptional equal-point cases are handled later.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: Moderate to high: the statement is largely recoverable, but several inequality and fraction glyphs are noisy, so formula-level use should be checked against the scan.

accepted_units.title: Nonzero constant discriminant forces local equalities
accepted_units.why_material: After deriving valuation inequalities from coordinate identities and the addition law, the proof represents the curve discriminant as a polynomial combination of the two partial derivatives. Because that nonzero discriminant lies in the constant field and has valuation zero, the possible strict inequalities would force a contradiction, upgrading the local estimates to the equalities in Lemma 2(a).
accepted_units.context_note: The span retains the preparatory coordinate identities, the three valuation cases, and the resultant argument; the conceptual mechanism is the constant discriminant acting as an obstruction to simultaneous positive valuation.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: High for exact algebra: identities (12)-(20) contain OCR loss, but the resultant representation and contradiction via w(D)=0 are explicit in prose and support the mechanism.

accepted_units.title: Closing the equal-pole case in characteristic 2 and non-2
accepted_units.why_material: The remaining part of Lemma 2 is reduced to unequal pole orders by Lemma 1, then treats equal pole orders through three possible valuations of P-Q and P+Q, using different coordinate identities in characteristic 2 and in other characteristics to obtain the missing equality.
accepted_units.context_note: This is the source's specific device for keeping the proof uniform across finite characteristics, the limitation highlighted in the introduction.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: High: several formulas and comparison glyphs are degraded; the case division and characteristic-dependent route are prose-recoverable, but exact computations require the scan.

accepted_units.title: Product-formula globalization of the parallelogram identity
accepted_units.why_material: The proof combines the mixed-sign case from Lemma 1, the local separation identities from Lemma 2, and the residue-degree-weighted product formula to show d(P-Q)+d(P+Q)=2d(P)+2d(Q), with the equal or opposite point cases supplied by doubling.
accepted_units.context_note: This is the decisive synthesis of the local valuation analysis into a quadratic form; it depends on the definitions and local lemmas rather than standing alone.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: High for the displayed summation chain, which is severely OCR-damaged; the prose explicitly names the inputs and conclusion, so only the semantic local-to-global mechanism is accepted.

accepted_units.title: Integer-lattice nonnegativity forces nonpositive discriminant
accepted_units.why_material: The source reduces positive semidefiniteness of each two-point restriction of d to a general lemma: if a real binary quadratic form is nonnegative on a scaled integer lattice, a positive discriminant would make the separation of its real roots grow with the lattice parameter while lattice nonnegativity bounds that separation, a contradiction.
accepted_units.context_note: Applying the lemma with unit scales is justified because d is a sum of nonnegative pole contributions; the concluding proposition records d as a positive semidefinite quadratic form.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: Low to moderate: a few symbols in the quadratic formulas are noisy, but the contradiction argument, application, and proposition are readable.

accepted_units.title: The Frobenius height matrix encodes the point-count error
accepted_units.why_material: For P0=(x,y) and its coordinatewise q-th-power Frobenius image Q0, Lemma 4 targets d(P0)=1, d(Q0)=q, and the cross term q-N; substituting these values into the nonpositive discriminant inequality is stated to be equivalent to the theorem's point-count bound.
accepted_units.context_note: This span is the explicit bridge from the general positive-semidefinite form to the arithmetic statement; the subsequent spans prove the three height values.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: Low to moderate: subscripts and some mathematical glyphs are noisy, but the three values and equivalence claim are legible.

accepted_units.title: The unique infinite prime gives the diagonal height values
accepted_units.why_material: The proof identifies the unique extension of the infinite prime to K through ramification degree two, computes the pole order of x there, and obtains d(P0)=1; Frobenius scaling similarly gives d(Q0)=q.
accepted_units.context_note: This isolates the diagonal terms of the Frobenius height matrix before the cross term is computed from finite and infinite primes.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: Moderate: the ramification calculation contains degraded notation, but its degree-two conclusion and the two d-values are explicit.

accepted_units.title: Rational solutions detected by primes dividing x-x^q
accepted_units.why_material: The addition formula shows that finite primes can create poles in x(P0+Q0) exactly when they divide x-x^q. The source then gives a bijection between k-solutions of the curve and degree-one primes with those residue coordinates, using the factorization of x^q-x to fix the positive valuation.
accepted_units.context_note: This span converts finite-field point counting into divisor data that can contribute to d(P0+Q0).
accepted_units.representation_dependency: Moderate to high: factorization (27) is truncated in the text layer, but the correspondence, its uniqueness, and valuation conclusion are stated in prose; exact factorization should be scan-checked.

accepted_units.title: Ramified degree-one primes contribute poles of order two
accepted_units.why_material: Among primes above factors of x^q-x, the ramified degree-one case uses the nonzero discriminant identity to keep one partial derivative a unit, determines the valuation of y-y^q, and hence obtains valuation -2 for the x-coordinate of P0+Q0; these primes account for M rational solutions.
accepted_units.context_note: This is the first branch of the finite-prime classification and reuses the discriminant obstruction from the local lemma proof.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: High: coordinate identities and exponent placement are OCR-damaged, but the ramified case, valuation -2, and definition of M are explicit; scan verification is needed for exact algebra.

accepted_units.title: Decomposed degree-one primes versus inert degree-two primes
accepted_units.why_material: The decomposed degree-one primes correspond to rational solutions but yield no negative x-valuation for P0+Q0, whereas inert degree-two primes yield no k-solution and contribute valuation -2; the source counts the two sets as 2L and q-L-M respectively.
accepted_units.context_note: Together with the ramified case, this separates point-count contribution from height contribution by residue degree and splitting behavior.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: Moderate: some residue-field notation is noisy, while the case distinctions, contribution signs, and counts are readable.

accepted_units.title: Prime-type counts produce the Frobenius cross term q-N
accepted_units.why_material: The classification gives N=2L+M. Adding the finite-prime contributions to the infinite-prime contribution in the definition of d yields the stated identity d(P0+Q0)-d(P0)-d(Q0)=q-N, completing Lemma 4 and therefore the theorem.
accepted_units.context_note: This is the terminal accounting step linking the divisor classification back to the discriminant reduction in lines 427-440.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: High for reconstructing the intermediate sum at lines 572-583, which is badly truncated; the count N=2L+M and final cross-term identity are legible, so the conclusion is accepted but exact arithmetic layout requires scan verification.
